title: Low-Frequency Quantitative Strategies in MetaTrader 5 (Part 6): A Constant-Dollar Exposure FX Trading System Based on Fixed-Income Interest Rate Yield Differentials
text:
Introduction
In 2014, Nicolas Georges, a hedge fund manager, proposed an intraday Forex trading system that does not depend on volume and is intended to work in both trending and ranging markets. Instead of relying on the usual carry-trading logic that uses government sovereign bond yields, he proposed using Interest Rate Swap (IRS) differential momentum to track currency pairs' relative variation. The system was called ANANTA.
The idea was pretty simple: instead of taking the central banks’ monetary policies as the main reference for currency portfolio management, let’s take the market expectations about the economies represented by those central banks. Instead of asking the governments how much interest rate they are willing to pay to finance their debt, let’s ask the people who buy that debt how much interest rate they think the government should offer. What are the commerce, the industry, the hedge fund managers, and other economic agents foreseeing for the economy?
A significant part of these economic agents’ answer is quoted live, all day long, on the interest rate swaps market. The system uses daily updated IRS data feeds to rebalance a portfolio of all G10 currencies plus the Danish krone (DKK).
“The G10 currencies are ten of the most heavily traded currencies in the world, which are also ten of the world's most liquid currencies. [...] There is no longer a one-to-one match between the G10 currencies and the G10 countries. [...] In some banking circles, reference is made to the G11 currencies, which are the G10 currencies plus the Danish krone (DKK).” (
Wikipedia
)
USD
- United States Dollar
EUR
- Euro
JPY
- Japanese Yen
GBP
- British Pound Sterling
CHF
- Swiss Franc
AUD - Australian Dollar *
CAD - Canadian Dollar
NZD - New Zealand Dollar *
SEK - Swedish Krona
NOK - Norwegian Krone *
DKK - Danish Krone
* Australia, New Zealand, and Norway are not part of the G10 countries. But their currencies are part of the world’s most liquid currencies.
In this article, we evaluate the system using only free IRS data feeds for the five most liquid G10 currencies: USD, Euro, GBP, JPY, and CHF.
Interest Rate Swap (IRS)
In the ANANTA system, we do not enter and exit the market according to trade signals. Instead, we stay continuously in the market, simply moving dollars from one currency to another. There is no stop-loss or volatility-based position resizing. Unlike the traditional carry trade setup of buying high-yielding currencies and selling the low-yielding ones, we use Interest Rate Swap (IRS) to gauge the short-term evolution of central banks' monetary policies. The author calls this the interest rate differential momentum.
“It is clear that the main influence on the foreign exchange market is the change in interest rates, guided by the central banks. With a slow rebalancing, this effect is captured by the carry trade. However, this paper will focus on the short-term impact of interest rate evolution, also called interest rate differential momentum.”
These IRS data feeds are NOT the same as government sovereign bond yields we can find for free on almost all central banks' websites and APIs. While the sovereign bond yields are tied to the issued government debt, the IRS is tied to OTC derivative contracts. They are different asset classes, and, what is more relevant for our trading system, they represent different market participants. While the sovereign bond yields reflect the central bank's monetary policy and are influenced by the central bank's own actions, the IRS is influenced by corporations and institutional investors, and reflects their reaction to those central bank policies, among other factors. Generally speaking, there is a regular spread between the sovereign bond yields and the IRS yields.
The system was developed in an institutional environment. It uses Bloomberg’s Composite London (CMPL) and Composite New York (CMPN) for spot currency rates. For interest rate yields, it sources data from Bloomberg’s composite swaps: ADSW2 (AUD), CDSW2 (CAD), SFSW2 (CHF), DKSW2 (DKK), EUSA2 (EUR), BPSW2 (GBP), JYSW2 (JPY), NKSW2 (NOK), NDSW2 (NZD), SKSW2 (SEK), and USSW2 (USD). These are real-time data feeds built from multiple contributors around the world and used to set the benchmark interest rate swaps. They are relatively expensive proprietary data feeds.
It makes no sense to propose an FX trading system evaluation that would be accessible only to those who can pay for data. We have found only one trustworthy source of free historical IRS data at
Investing.com
. However, it does not include all G11 currencies; only the most liquid ones: USD, euro, GBP, JPY, and CHF. These are the currencies we are using in the backtests that follow.
What if you have access to IRS data for AUD, CAD, NZD, NOK, and DKK? If you have access to this data and want to run an evaluation with all G10 currencies, you can just include them via the
InpCustomUniverse
input parameter. The Expert Advisor is ready to accept the inclusion of any other IRS data feed, provided their CSV files follow the same data shape and formatting used in the samples attached at the bottom of the article.

Implementation
The current implementation is composed of seven headers, besides the main Expert Advisor. Five of these headers contain the following components:
Regular MQL5 definitions (Defines.mqh),
support functions, such as reading CSV files (CsvYieldReader.mqh), or managing the synchronization between the broker server time and the London Stock Exchange closing time (RebalanceTimer.mqh),
and order triggering (TradeExecution.mqh) or position sizing (PortfolioExposure.mqh).
The core strategy implementation is distributed between
YieldMatrix.mqh
and SignalEngine.mqh.
By examining these two files, we can clearly see how the system works.
The system’s trading hypothesis is that, instead of trading central banks' interest rates, as the traditional carry trade does, we can trade the interest rate expectations for a given time horizon, a 2-year time horizon, in this case. The 2-year interest rate swap reflects the collective market
expectations
of where the interest rate will be over the next two years. So, our first step is to compare each country's 2-year IRS with each other country’s IRS and calculate the spread between each of them.
Fig 1 - Interest Rate Swap (IRS) differential formula (simple subtraction)
Where i and j are countries and j > i. It is a simple subtraction operation that gives us the raw spread (IRS differential). For example, if the US 2-year yield is 4.95% and the Eurozone 2-year yield is 3.42%,
diff(EUR,USD)=4.95 − 3.42 = +1.53%
Throughout this article, for a pair (ccy1, ccy2), we define
diff(ccy1, ccy2) = yield(ccy2) - yield(ccy1)
Therefore, a positive momentum signal favors ccy2 over ccy1 in the page-4 momentum logic used here.

Continuing with the example above, is an IRS differential of +1.53% bullish or bearish for the Euro? Unlike sovereign bond yields, for this strategy, the raw differential is interpreted relative to its recent history rather than in absolute terms. For the current spread to have significance, we need context: how does it compare to recent days? To make sense of this IRS differential's relative significance, we calculate a Simple Moving Average (SMA) of its values for the last X days.
Fig. 2 – IRS differential SMA formula
Where X=2 for the short-term model, and X=15 for the long-term model. If X=2, the moving average is just the average of today’s spread and yesterday’s spread.
Fig. 3 – Average spread formula

The sub-signal absolute value tells us how unusual the movement is. The sign tells us its direction.
+100% means the difference is much higher than its recent average.
+33% means it is somewhat higher than its average.
-33% means it is lower than its average.
The negative sign says that the Day 2 difference moved downward relative to its recent average.
It is easy to see that each pair will produce sub-signals every single business day. However, we do not want to trade every single sub-signal. That would be inefficient. The transaction costs, spreads, and commissions would eat most of our profit, and most of the sub-signals are nothing more than market noise. To avoid making our strategy unprofitable due to excessive transaction costs, we need to filter these sub-signals to trade only those that reflect an IRS spread change large enough to cover the costs of moving our capital from one currency pair to another. The system uses the 50th percentile as a threshold. We will discard the bottom 50% of the weakest signals and keep only the strongest ones, the top 50%.
For our purposes here, we can use the median as the 50th percentile and use the Alglib::SampleMedian function from the
MQL5 Alglib native implementation

The practical effect of this 50th-percentile filter is easy to understand. Let’s suppose these absolute sub-signal sizes: 10%, 20%, 33%, 50%, and 100%. The middle value (50th percentile) is 33%. The 10% and 20% sub-signals are discarded. We only keep the 33%, 50%, and 100% sub-signals. These sub-signals are aggregated into the final individual currency positions (+1/-1) against the USD, because it is our reference currency. The netting rule is that: for a positive pair signal, the first currency receives +1 and the second receives -1. For a negative pair signal, the first receives -1 and the second receives +1.
Positive sub-signal: EUR gets +1, USD gets -1
Negative sub-signal: EUR gets -1, USD gets +1
The +1 and -1 are directions, not percentages.

A summary of the process:
We start with pairwise IRS differences.
Then, we calculate a 2-day (or 15-day) moving average for each difference and normalize the results into a sub-signal.
Next, we
get the 50th percentile
of the absolute sub-signals and discard those below it to trade only the strongest movements.
Finally, we
net (add and subtract) the directions
for each non-USD currency.
This will give us a rebalancing table like this, which will be printed on the MetaTrader 5 log:
Fig. 6 - Final rebalancing signal example printed on the MetaTrader 5 log
In this example, JPY appears as a base or quote currency in four pairs that passed the 50th percentile filter, and all contributions were positive. Again, the totals are NOT percentages and NOT direct trade sizes. They are direction counts. The greater the absolute number, the greater the number of pair signals that contributed in that direction, like points in a game. A greater positive number indicates more points to buy against the dollar; conversely, a greater negative number indicates more points to sell against the dollar.
At the end, we will have 4 non-USD currency signals for portfolio rebalancing.
FX spot data and IRS data alignment
Because we are dealing with data from several territories, no matter where we source our data from, or which timeframe we are operating on, the data is subject to misalignment when one of the sources has no data for a given timestamp. It can be due to an expected reason, like a local bank holiday, or it can be due to unexpected data gaps.
The class CYieldMatrix produces an aligned chronological calendar and forward-fills the latest available closing yields for any data gap.

The portfolio rebalancing frequency
The original system rechecks the G10 currencies portfolio twice a day for rebalancing at London and New York close. The London close is the main checkpoint when the bulk of changes are made. The New York close allows for small adjustments or to capture eventual late-day interest rate shocks.
“[...] the rebalancing is done in 2 steps: a first snapshot of the interest data at the London close and rebalancing the portfolio at that time (this also coincides with the maximum of liquidity in the FX market and more aggressive spreads), then a second snapshot at the New York close and readjusting again. Variations in interest rate differentials tend to be limited between London close and New York close times, making the adjustments at  New York time marginal. In the event of a major move in interest rates just before New York closes, a more substantial adjustment of the portfolio will take place.”
Since the free data we are using is updated only once a day, our backtests are checking for rebalances once a day too, on the London close.

The backtest
The author of the original system trading all G10 currencies reported a Sharpe Ratio of 1.81 for the short-model and 1.63 for the long-model. They have backtested for ten years (2003 - 2013). We verified a slightly better Sharpe Ratio with only the most liquid currencies for the last six and a half years (2020 - Oct, 2026).

We let the EA use its input parameter defaults, the same settings you will find in the backtest settings INI file attached in the article. Since we are backtesting in the daily timeframe, we used “1 minute OHLC” modelling to speed up the first check. But we repeated the backtest with “every tick” modelling, just in case (see below).

Conclusion
In this article, we evaluated ANANTA, a quantitative Forex trading system that tracks fixed-income interest rate swap variation to estimate currencies’ buying or selling pressure. Instead of trading each pair individually, the original system operates by rebalancing a constant-dollar exposure portfolio of G10 currencies.
In this implementation, due to our self-imposed requirement of only using free IRS data sources, we restricted the currency pairs to the five most liquid ones: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, and CHF. We also changed the original system’s twice-a-day rebalancing to once-a-day rebalancing, since our free IRS data source is only updated once a day.
The system showed stable equity growth, with a Sharpe Ratio of 2.41, a Z-Score of 3.60, and a max balance drawdown of ~11%.
The current implementation is flexible enough to accommodate the full currency universe by adding one configuration line per currency.
The IRS data used in the backtests are compiled in CSV files attached to the article for easy reproduction of the experiment.

for: Formula for IRS differential: diff(ccy1, ccy2) = yield(ccy2) - yield(ccy1), used as raw input for momentum calculation
Momentum defined as (current_diff - avg) / |avg|, where avg is the 2-day SMA of the differential series — explicitly called 'IRS momentum' and tied to short-term interest rate evolution
50th percentile (median) filter applied to absolute sub-signals to discard bottom 50% — described as a noise-reduction mechanism to cover transaction costs and avoid unprofitable trades
Rebalancing triggered daily at London close (16:00 UTC) using aligned, forward-filled IRS data — timing and alignment protocol specified to ensure reproducible, timestamp-consistent signal generation
Backtest results report Sharpe Ratio of 2.41, Z-Score of 3.60, and max balance drawdown ~11% over 2020–2026 — empirical performance metrics derived from historical application of the full rule set

against: The system uses daily updated IRS data feeds that are not available for spot-forex traders in real time — specifically, free IRS data from Investing.com is used, but the article admits it is incomplete (only 5 of 11 currencies), and the full implementation relies on Bloomberg’s proprietary composite IRS feeds (e.g., USSW2, EUSA2) which are 'relatively expensive proprietary data feeds' — this violates condition (3): 'need data which is not available for spot-forex', because Bloomberg IRS feeds (CMPL/CMPN spot rates + composite swaps) are institutional OTC derivative benchmarks, not observable or replicable from standard spot-forex price/time/volume data; no formula is given to reconstruct IRS yields from spot FX or OHLC data.

The rebalancing logic depends on aligned calendar dates built from IRS CSV files (via CYieldMatrix::BuildUnifiedCalendar), which forward-fills missing IRS values — but the alignment procedure relies on *external, non-synchronized, non-forex-native timestamps* (e.g., London Stock Exchange closing time, bank holidays, territory-specific trading days) and performs forward-fill interpolation across heterogeneous sources — this introduces a non-reproducible, non-deterministic dependency: the resulting 'unified calendar' and filled yields depend on the exact set and completeness of the input CSVs, and cannot be computed solely from closed FX bars (OHLC), time, spread, or tick volume — violating condition (2): 'cannot write exact formula for feature or rule based only on closed bars'.

The signal generation requires computing the 50th percentile (median) of absolute sub-signals across *all active currency pairs* at each rebalance — this is a cross-sectional rank-based filter over a dynamic universe (configurable via InpCustomUniverse), meaning the threshold p50 depends on the full set of pairwise differentials *at that date*, including pairs whose IRS data may be missing or interpolated — while median computation itself is deterministic, the *input set* is not defined by a fixed formula over bar data but by external CSV availability and calendar alignment logic — thus the filter is not expressible as a closed-form function of prices/spread/time/tick-volume alone, failing condition (2).
non_fatal: No out-of-sample validation is shown — only in-sample backtest results (2020–2026) are reported.
No accounting for variable spreads or commissions in the backtest — only 'every tick' vs 'OHLC' modelling is compared.

The position sizing uses constant-dollar exposure, but the article does not specify how lot size is calculated under varying margin requirements or pip-value shifts — this is an implementation detail, not a conceptual flaw.

The system assumes daily IRS updates at London close, but real-world IRS data releases have irregular timing (e.g., lagged, revised, or delayed); the article does not address revision risk or data latency.

judge.reject_reason: Фатальный порок: система требует данных, недоступных на спот-форексе — конкретно, ежедневные IRS-ставки с Bloomberg (например, USSW2, EUSA2), которые являются проприетарными OTC-деривативными бенчмарками, не наблюдаемыми и неприменимыми из стандартных OHLC/спред/тик-объём/время. Статья прямо признаёт, что бесплатные данные с Investing.com неполны (только 5 из 11 валют), а полная реализация зависит от дорогостоящих институциональных источников. Нет формулы для восстановления IRS-ставок из цен спот-форекса или закрытых баров. Также невозможно записать детерминированное правило входа или признак только по закрытым барам: алгоритм выравнивания календаря (CYieldMatrix::BuildUnifiedCalendar) использует внешние, несинхронизированные, территориально-зависимые временные метки (праздники, время закрытия LSE), а также forward-fill интерполяцию по CSV-файлам — это создаёт недетерминированную, неповторяемую зависимость от внешних данных, не выводимых из цен, спреда, тик-объёма или времени по закрытым барам. Кросс-секционный медианный фильтр (50-й перцентиль) зависит от динамического набора пар и их интерполированных значений — входной набор не определяется фиксированной формулой по барам, а зависит от доступности и полноты внешних CSV, что делает фильтр непредставимым как Feature_Or_Filter или Strategy в рамках условий.

judge.summary: Статья описывает систему ANANTA, использующую дифференциалы ставок по свопам процентных ставок (IRS) для ребалансировки портфеля валют. Однако её реализация полностью зависит от внешних, проприетарных и ненаблюдаемых на спот-форексе данных, а логика выравнивания календаря и медианного фильтра не может быть выражена детерминированной формулой по закрытым барам.
